topic: Induction & Airway Management in Neurosurgical Patients
domain: Neuroanesthesia (craniotomy, ICP, cerebral protection, neuromonitoring, awake craniotomy, spine surgery)
stem: When is airway management typically indicated in a deteriorating traumatic brain injury patient?
answer: Airway management is usually indicated when GCS falls to 8 or below or with concurrent injuries requiring airway protection
rationale: GCS of 8 or less indicates inability to protect the airway from aspiration and impending respiratory failure, requiring immediate intubation.
confusable_with: Waiting for GCS to reach 3 before intubating

topic: Induction & Airway Management in Neurosurgical Patients
domain: Neuroanesthesia (craniotomy, ICP, cerebral protection, neuromonitoring, awake craniotomy, spine surgery)
stem: Why should nasal airways and nasogastric tubes be avoided in patients with suspected basal skull fracture?
answer: Nasal airways and NGTs should be avoided with suspected basal skull fracture due to risk of intracranial placement
rationale: A fracture at the base of the skull allows passage of nasally inserted devices through the fracture into the intracranial compartment.
confusable_with: Nasal airways being safe if no visible facial trauma

topic: Induction & Airway Management in Neurosurgical Patients
domain: Neuroanesthesia (craniotomy, ICP, cerebral protection, neuromonitoring, awake craniotomy, spine surgery)
stem: What TBI management principle regarding airway pressure is applied during RSI?
answer: During RSI for TBI, positive pressure less than 20 cmH2O is used if mask ventilation is necessary to limit ICP elevation
rationale: High positive pressure during bag-mask ventilation impairs venous return, raising ICP; limiting pressure minimises secondary brain injury.
confusable_with: High-pressure mask ventilation being necessary to prevent hypoxia in TBI

topic: Induction & Airway Management in Neurosurgical Patients
domain: Neuroanesthesia (craniotomy, ICP, cerebral protection, neuromonitoring, awake craniotomy, spine surgery)
stem: Propofol has what clinically useful property in patients with COPD relevant to induction?
answer: Propofol can produce bronchodilation in patients with COPD (and inhibits pulmonary vasoconstriction)
rationale: Propofol reduces airway reactivity by inhibiting vagal-mediated bronchoconstriction, making it advantageous for induction in COPD and reactive airway disease.

topic: Induction & Airway Management in Neurosurgical Patients
domain: Neuroanesthesia (craniotomy, ICP, cerebral protection, neuromonitoring, awake craniotomy, spine surgery)
stem: What laryngoscopic grading system classifies intubation difficulty based on the view obtained?
answer: Cormack and Lehane classification (Grades I-IV); Grades III and IV are associated with difficult intubation
rationale: Grade III (only epiglottis visible) and Grade IV (no glottic structures visible) predict failed direct laryngoscopy and trigger advanced airway techniques.
confusable_with: Mallampati score (pharyngeal view with mouth open, before laryngoscopy)

topic: Infraclavicular and axillary brachial plexus blocks
domain: Regional anesthesia & acute pain (neuraxial, peripheral nerve blocks, ultrasound guidance, acute pain service, multimodal analgesia, LAST, complications)
stem: For surgeries distal to the mid-humerus, which brachial plexus block approaches are recommended?
answer: Supraclavicular, infraclavicular, and axillary approaches are recommended for surgeries distal to the mid-humerus
rationale: These distal brachial plexus approaches block the terminal nerve branches more reliably for forearm and hand surgery than more proximal interscalene block.
confusable_with: Interscalene block for all upper extremity surgeries (misses ulnar nerve distribution)

topic: Infraclavicular and axillary brachial plexus blocks
domain: Regional anesthesia & acute pain (neuraxial, peripheral nerve blocks, ultrasound guidance, acute pain service, multimodal analgesia, LAST, complications)
stem: What are the few contraindications to axillary brachial plexus block?
answer: Local infection at the injection site is a contraindication to axillary brachial plexus block
rationale: Injecting through infected tissue risks seeding the perineural sheath with bacteria; other contraindications include patient refusal and coagulopathy.
confusable_with: Anticoagulation being an absolute contraindication to all peripheral blocks

topic: Infraclavicular and axillary brachial plexus blocks
domain: Regional anesthesia & acute pain (neuraxial, peripheral nerve blocks, ultrasound guidance, acute pain service, multimodal analgesia, LAST, complications)
stem: Why is the axilla a suboptimal site for a perineural catheter compared to infraclavicular placement?
answer: Axillary perineural catheters provide inferior analgesia and have increased infection and displacement risks compared to infraclavicular catheters
rationale: The axilla is mobile with skin folds promoting bacterial colonisation and catheter movement; infraclavicular position is more anatomically stable.
confusable_with: Axillary catheter being equivalent to infraclavicular for continuous block

topic: Infraclavicular and axillary brachial plexus blocks
domain: Regional anesthesia & acute pain (neuraxial, peripheral nerve blocks, ultrasound guidance, acute pain service, multimodal analgesia, LAST, complications)
stem: What ultrasound-guided approaches are most recommended for brachial plexus blocks due to ease of ultrasound guidance?
answer: Axillary, supraclavicular, and infraclavicular blocks are most readily performed using ultrasound guidance
rationale: These approaches have superficial nerve locations with consistent sonographic anatomy, making ultrasound guidance reliable and reducing complication rates.
confusable_with: Interscalene block being the easiest to guide with ultrasound (deeper, more variable anatomy)

topic: Infraclavicular and axillary brachial plexus blocks
domain: Regional anesthesia & acute pain (neuraxial, peripheral nerve blocks, ultrasound guidance, acute pain service, multimodal analgesia, LAST, complications)
stem: What property of regional anesthesia in addition to potent analgesia may benefit patients beyond pain control?
answer: Regional anesthesia may reduce the neuroendocrine stress response, systemic opioid requirements, and associated opioid-related adverse effects
rationale: Blocking afferent nociceptive signals attenuates cortisol/catecholamine release, reducing cardiac stress and improving postoperative recovery.
confusable_with: Regional anesthesia benefiting only pain scores without systemic effects
